[Pillow] Pillow: Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
items.summary: ============================================================================Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memoryLocation: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216  in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's Image.quantize(palette=...), the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary.The bug is in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() in src/libImaging/Palette.c. It fills a local UINT8 c[512] only inside loops bounded by palette->size. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. topalette() in src/libImaging/Convert.c then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. topalette() rejects a NULL palette but not one with size == 0. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry "P" image: a PNG with a zero-length PLTE chunk opened with Image.open(), a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare Image.new("P", ...). The attacker must control the palette image; the source image can be anything, and RGB sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. The attached reproducer quantizes a 512-colour strip against the empty-palette PNG and finds 8 of the 64 output words pointing into the process's own [stack] mapping, while a one-entry palette control yields all zeros. The behaviour was introduced in commit 54cb09d8b48c (first released in 9.1.0). The Image.new("P", ...) route exists since 10.1.0.DetailsImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() (src/libImaging/Palette.c:154) computes, for one 8×8×8 box of the colour cache, the nearest palette index for each of the 512 slots into a local UINT8 c[512] and then copies c[] into the cache. c[] is only ever written inside for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++). When the palette has zero entries nothing writes it, the untouched stack bytes are copied into the cache, and topalette() (src/libImaging/Convert.c:1145) emits them as the output pixels of Image.quantize(palette=...). The root cause is that topalette() only rejects a NULL palette, never one with palette->size == 0, while ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() silently assumes size >= 1. A zero-entry "P" image is what Image.open() produces for a PNG whose PLTE chunk has length 0 (or a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0); Image.new("P", size) without a subsequent putpalette() yields one as well. Both dither modes (Dither.NONE and the default Floyd-Steinberg) are affected for RGB sources (an L source takes the grayscale copy path and never consults the cache).Showing it with the installed build, no special flags. The 80-byte PNG below is 4×4, bit depth 8, colour type 3, with a zero-length PLTE and an all-zero IDAT:89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 0000000400000004 0803000000 9e2f6e4c00000000 504c5445 4ba889550000000b 49444154 789c6360c0040000140001 7dfe1eee00000000 49454e44 ae426082pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); pal.load()      # pal.mode == "P", pal.im.getpalette("RGB") == b""src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1))src.putdata([(r*4, g*4, b*4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)])out = src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE)out.tobytes()        # 512 bytes, different in every processThe 512 source colours are chosen so that each pixel lands in a distinct slot of the cache box for r,g,b ∈ [0,32), in slot order, so out.tobytes() is exactly c[0..511]. Read as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and resolved against the same process's /proc/self/maps, a typical run gives 43 words that are addresses inside the process's own mappings — 8 in [stack], several in [heap], libc.so.6, libpython3.12.so and _imaging.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so — and 3 words equal to the thread's stack-protector canary (read from fs:0x28 for comparison). The same PNG with a 3-byte PLTE (one entry) gives 512 zero bytes in every run. out.save(buf, "PNG") succeeds, so the bytes leave the process in an ordinary image. Under valgrind (run against a strip --strip-debug copy of _imaging.so or a gcc build, since valgrind 3.19 cannot read clang's DWARF5) the report carries the origin Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate. With Dither.NONE topalette only copies the bytes, so the first use of uninitialised value is flagged where Python first branches on the pixel data; with the default Floyd-Steinberg dither it is flagged inside topalette

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open()
items.summary:
============================================================================Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open()Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266  in GifImageFile._seek()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Opening a crafted GIF file with Image.open() takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside Image.open() itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format.The bug is in GifImageFile._seek() in src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py, which builds info["comment"] by appending to an immutable bytes object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (comment += block, line 261) and once per comment extension (info["comment"] += b"
" + comment, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because _open() ends with self._seek(0), any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached.DetailsGifImageFile._seek() collects GIF comment extensions into info["comment"] using bytes concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. bytes is immutable, so every += allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by Image.open() is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0.A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension 21 FE 01 41 00 repeated makes this directly observable. Image.open(BytesIO(data)) on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine:file sizecomment extensions (21 FE …)same bytes labelled plain-text extension (21 01 …)1 MB1.2 s0.09 s2 MB4.9 s0.13 s4 MB35 s0.26 s8 MB183 s—The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from 0xFE to 0x01; it goes through the same loop and the same self.data() reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No load() is needed and no warning or exception is raised; im.info["comment"] simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob.The code, src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281 (trimmed):            elif s == b"!":                s = self.fp.read(1)                block = self.data()                …                elif s[0] == 254:                    #                    # comment extension                    #                    comment = b""                    # Read this comment block                    while block:                        comment += block                      # :261  one copy per sub-block                        block = self.data()                    if "comment" in info:                        # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with 
                        info["comment"] += b"
" + comment    # :266  one copy per extension                    else:                        info["comment"] = comment                    s = b""                    continue                …                while self.data():                            # every other extension: read and drop                    passself.data() (:97-102) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two += lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of info["comment"] once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doublin

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF
items.summary: ============================================================================Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDsLocation: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86  in MicImageFile.tell()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional olefile package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads im.n_frames can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with save_all=True to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it.The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. MicImageFile subclasses TiffImageFile and overrides seek() and tell() so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with self._seek(self.tell() + 1) until _n_frames is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress:MicImageFile.tell() (src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86) returns the constant stream index.MicImageFile.seek() calls TiffImageFile._open(), which resets _n_frames to None.As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. Image.open(), load(), thumbnail(), convert(), is_animated and ImageSequence iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed MicImageFile's own n_frames property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds.DetailsMicImageFile (registered for Image.open whenever olefile is installed) subclasses TiffImageFile and redefines a "frame" as one OLE *.ACI/Image stream, overriding seek() and tell() accordingly. It does not override the n_frames property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on tell() advancing as IFDs are loaded. MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside n_frames, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever.A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose img0.ACI/Image stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. Image.open() on it succeeds (format MIC, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating im.n_frames then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is  File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup  File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek  File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_framesand instrumenting _seek shows it being called with frame=1, tell()==0, _frame_pos==[8, 122], _n_frames is None on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give n_frames == 3 in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives n_frames == 1.The loop, src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212:    @property    def n_frames(self) -> int:        current_n_frames = self._n_frames        if current_n_frames is None:            current = self.tell()            self._seek(len(self._frame_pos))            while self._n_frames is None:                self._seek(self.tell() + 1)      # 1219            self.seek(current)and the overrides that break its progress assumption, src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76:    def seek(self, frame: int) -> None:        …        self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename)        TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)   # 82: resets _n_frames to None        self.frame = frame    def tell(self) -> int:        return self.frame                            # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frameFor a plain TIFF, _seek(k) (TiffImagePlugin.py:1236) loads IFDs up to k, appending each offset to _frame_pos, setting _n_frames when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private __frame = k; TiffImageFile.tell() returns __frame, so self.tell() + 1 walks the chain to its end.For a MIC file, Image.open → MicImageFile._open sets self._n_frames = len(self.images) at line 69, but then calls self.seek(0) → TiffImageFile._open (line 82), which unconditionally sets self._n_frames = None (TiffImagePlugin.py:1203) and _seek(0)s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so _n_frames stays None after open. n_frames then runs: current = self.tell() is 0 (the OLE index); _seek(len(_frame_pos)) = _seek(1) loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also n

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment copying during save
items.summary: On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream main (ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9), a GIF with a long comment makes _get_global_header() copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional Moderate severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-fc9g-5qg7-mf45https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112891https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/68a3fe957d8a4d552e8c69d96066d749f0614c7ehttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fc9g-5qg7-mf45

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images
items.summary: ============================================================================NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size imagesLocation: src/libImaging/Filter.c:79  in ImagingExpand()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================Applying Pillow's median, minimum, maximum or rank filter to an image with zero width or zero height crashes the whole Python process instead of raising an error. Empty images like this are easy to produce with ordinary calls, for example a crop box whose left and right edges (or top and bottom edges) are equal, or the second page of a crafted multi-page image file. An attacker who can supply crop coordinates or an uploaded file to an application that runs one of these filters can kill its worker process. The effect is a crash only, with no memory disclosure or corruption.The fault is in ImagingExpand() in src/libImaging/Filter.c. This is the edge-padding step that RankFilter.filter() always runs through the core expand() method, so MedianFilter, MinFilter and MaxFilter go through it too. It fills the margin by copying the input's edge pixels, reading imIn->image[y][0] and rows 0 / ysize-1, and never checks that the input has any pixels. For an empty image, ImagingAllocateArray leaves the line pointers NULL, so the first read dereferences NULL and the process dies with SIGSEGV, in every mode.Zero-size images reach this point through public API alone:Image.crop(), ImageOps.crop() and Image.new();a multi-page TIFF opened by path whose second IFD declares ImageLength = 0, on which seek(1) and load() succeed.Every other ImageFilter returns an empty image for the same inputs. The zero-height case has crashed since the original PIL import, and the zero-width case since Pillow 4.3.0. This is separate from the margin == 0 fix in #9755: the path is the same, but here the degenerate value is the image size rather than the kernel size. It has the same shape as the zero-dimension ImagingOffset crash fixed under GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w.The attached reproducer shows a one-pixel-wide control crop filtering normally, while four empty crops passed through the rank filters are each killed by SIGSEGV. A patch that returns early in ImagingExpand for empty input is included.DetailsImagingExpand() (src/libImaging/Filter.c), the edge-padding helper that ImageFilter.RankFilter runs before the actual rank filter, reads the first pixel of each input line without checking that the input has any pixels. For an image with width 0 or height 0 the line pointers are NULL, so Image.filter() with MedianFilter, MinFilter, MaxFilter or RankFilter kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV instead of returning or raising:from PIL import Image, ImageFilterim = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop((3, 0, 3, 10))   # size (0, 10); crop() accepts left == rightim.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))               # SIGSEGVUnder gdb on the stock build the fault is at ImagingExpand (imIn=…, margin=1) at src/libImaging/Filter.c:105 (the EXPAND(UINT8, image8) expansion), called from _expand_image at src/_imaging.c:1151, with imIn->xsize = 0 and imIn->image[0] = 0x0. The same happens for every mode the rank filters accept (L, RGB, RGBA, I, F), and the core expand(m) method with m >= 1 crashes the same way in any mode, including P. The same input through BoxBlur, GaussianBlur, Kernel, ModeFilter and UnsharpMask returns a (0, 10) image; a (1, 10) crop through MedianFilter also returns normally.The unchecked edge reads date from the PIL import (9a640e315, 2010, so every Pillow release): the zero-height case has crashed since then, and the zero-width case since fd907fbdc ("Fix 0-width and 0-height images other way", Pillow 4.3.0), which stopped backing zero-width images with a dummy block and left their row pointers NULL. It is adjacent to the margin == 0 divide-by-zero fix in #9755 — same expand() → ImagingExpand() path, but the unhandled degenerate value here is the image size rather than the kernel size.The path:# src/PIL/ImageFilter.py:111-116   RankFilter.filter  (MedianFilter/MinFilter/MaxFilter subclass it)        image = image.expand(self.size // 2)        return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank)expand(m) with m > 0 is ImagingExpand(self->image, m) (src/_imaging.c:1142-1151). It validates only margin, allocates an output of (xsize+2*margin) × (ysize+2*margin) — which is non-empty, so the allocation succeeds — and then fills the margin by replicating edge pixels of the input:// src/libImaging/Filter.c:70-101    imOut =        ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin);    …#define EXPAND_LINE(type, image, yin, yout)                       \    {                                                             \        for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) {                            \            imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0];          \   // line 79        }

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: NULL pointer dereference in Image.merge via an unvalidated band 0
items.summary: SummaryImage.merge() checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band I or F image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain Image.open() followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.DetailsThe validation loop skips band 0:src/PIL/Image.py:3795 iterates for band in bands[1:] and checks mode and size only for those.For an I or F image the 8-bit plane image8 is NULL (only image32 is set). ImagingMerge dereferences bands[0]->image8[y] for the multi-band output modes:src/libImaging/Bands.c:302, :311, :321The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169 registers the opener with no accept function.PoCfrom PIL import Image# Band 0 is a single-band "I" image: its image8 plane is NULL. merge() validates only# bands[1:], so the native ImagingMerge dereferences the NULL plane for band 0.band0 = Image.new("I", (4, 4))Image.merge("RGB", [band0, Image.new("L", (4, 4)), Image.new("L", (4, 4))])Run it:$ python 02_poc.pySegmentation fault (core dumped)Observed on a source build of commit 3e2ab96.Under AddressSanitizer:==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000    #0 ImagingMerge   src/libImaging/Bands.c:311    #1 _merge         src/_imaging.c:2492SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/libImaging/Bands.c:311 in ImagingMergeThe null address confirms the dereference of the missing image8 plane for band 0.ImpactNULL pointer dereference in a C extension. A crafted file opened and loaded through the IPTC path crashes the worker process. This is a hard crash, not a Python exception an application can catch.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-cp9v-662q-vvx9https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112405https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/b6ee66e8b2c2c0932bdf65f963268d9f2927ef86https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cp9v-662q-vvx9

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Invalid free in FreeType glyph rendering when a stroker is active
items.summary: SummaryWhen text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If FT_Load_Glyph fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls FT_Done_Glyph on the glyph variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.Detailsglyph is declared without a NULL initializer:src/_imagingft.c:848The first measurement loop can jump to glyph_error before glyph is ever assigned:src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:src/_imagingft.c:1242The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256ImageFont.truetype accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.PoCThis needs fontTools and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so FT_Load_Glyph returns an error while the face still opens.import structfrom fontTools.ttLib import TTFontfrom PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDrawSRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a basett = TTFont(SRC)gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")])loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormattt.close()raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read())nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0]tbl = {}for i in range(nt):    rec = 12 + i * 16    tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")    off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])    tbl[tag] = (off, length)glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0]if loca_long:    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0]else:    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opensd = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64)))d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointerResult on the pinned build: FT_Load_Glyph returns an error and execution reaches the glyph_error cleanup that calls FT_Done_Glyph(glyph) (the plugin surfaces OSError: invalid outline).ImpactApplications that draw text with stroke_width != 0 using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize glyph = NULL and set it back to NULL after each FT_Done_Glyph.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-j4m9-6w36-pw47https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112893https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/a7416de7f3a43128179d2cf68df3240ea8dafe13https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j4m9-6w36-pw47

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Double free in ImagingScaleAffine on calloc failure via Image.transform
items.summary: ============================================================================Double free in ImagingScaleAffine on calloc failure via Image.transformLocation: src/libImaging/Geometry.c:866  in ImagingScaleAffine()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================There is a double free in Pillow's Image.transform() that crashes the process when an oversized transform runs out of memory. Instead of only raising MemoryError, Pillow frees the output image's memory once while handling the error and then again when the Python object is cleaned up. Anyone who can choose the output size of Image.transform() can trigger it, but only on a worker with a memory limit (a common hardening for image workers) or a 32-bit process. The result is a crash of the worker, plus corruption of its heap that has not been shown to be controllable.The bug is in ImagingScaleAffine() in src/libImaging/Geometry.c (line 866). When its calloc() for the per-column lookup table of 4 × width bytes fails, it calls ImagingDelete(imOut). When the call comes from Image.transform(), imOut is the Imaging struct owned by the live Python ImagingCore output object. _dealloc() in src/_imaging.c later runs ImagingDelete() on the freed struct again, writing its mutex and refcount in freed memory and freeing the pixel blocks a second time. The path is reached with Transform.EXTENT, or Transform.AFFINE with a pure scale/translate matrix, under the default NEAREST resampling. A very wide, 1-row output size makes the lookup table the allocation that fails while the image itself still fits. On 64-bit Linux with default overcommit, that requires an address-space limit such as ulimit -v, uwsgi --limit-as or systemd LimitAS=. resize(), thumbnail() and rotate() are not affected. The attached reproducer runs on a stock build with a 1 GB limit: transform((300000000, 1), EXTENT) raises and catches MemoryError, then the process dies with SIGSEGV in free() called from _dealloc(). A memory-checking build reports the same path as a heap use-after-free. The faulty line was inherited from PIL 1.1.7 in the original fork commit, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected. A patch is attached.DetailsImagingScaleAffine() frees an image it does not own. On the one error path where its calloc() for the per-column lookup table fails, it calls ImagingDelete(imOut). When reached through Image.transform(), imOut is the Imaging struct held by a live Python ImagingCore object; that object's _dealloc() later calls ImagingDelete() on the already-freed struct and frees its pixel blocks a second time.Shortest demonstration on the stock build (the address-space limit stands in for ulimit -v / uwsgi --limit-as / systemd LimitAS= on a worker):import resource, gcfrom PIL import Imageresource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (1_000_000_000,) * 2)src = Image.new("L", (8, 8))try:    src.transform((300_000_000, 1), Image.Transform.EXTENT, (0, 0, 8, 8))except MemoryError:    pass                      # expected, and the process should carry ongc.collect()                  # instead: SIGSEGV in _dealloc -> ImagingDelete -> free()The 300 MB output image allocates; calloc(300000000, 4) (1.2 GB) does not. MemoryError is raised as intended, but the interpreter then dies with SIGSEGV, gdb showing free() ← memory_return_block/ImagingDestroyArray (src/libImaging/Storage.c:396,408) ← ImagingDelete (Storage.c:271) ← _dealloc (src/_imaging.c:188). An AddressSanitizer build of the same sources (with max_allocation_size_mb used to make the calloc fail instead of an rlimit) reports heap-use-after-free in ImagingDelete src/libImaging/Storage.c:257 called from _dealloc src/_imaging.c:188, on a 128-byte region "freed by" ImagingDelete ← ImagingScaleAffine src/libImaging/Geometry.c:866 ← ImagingTransformAffine Geometry.c:1043 ← ImagingTransform Geometry.c:1135 ← _transform src/_imaging.c:2153, "previously allocated by" ImagingNewPrologueSubtype Storage.c:53 ← … ← _new src/_imaging.c:756.Code pathImage.transform() creates the output image as an ordinary Python-owned image and then transforms into it:# src/PIL/Image.py:3008…3021        im = new(self.mode, size, fillcolor)        …            im.__transformer(                (0, 0, *size), self, method, data, resample, fillcolor is None            )__transformer() rewrites Transform.EXTENT into an axis-aligned affine matrix (src/PIL/Image.py:3040-3046: data = (xs, 0, x0, 0, ys, y0), method = Transform.AFFINE) and calls self.im.transform(box, image.im, method, data, resample, fill) (Image.py:3117). resample defaults to Resampling.NEAREST (Image.py:2936).In C, _transform() passes its own image as the destination:/* src/_imaging.c:2153 */    imOut = ImagingTransform(        self->image, imagep->image, method, x0, y0, x1, y1, a, filter, fill    );ImagingTransformAffine() takes the scaling fast path because the filter is NEAREST and the matrix has no shear:/* src/libImaging/Geometry.c:1035-1043 */

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: P;2L and P;4L decoders may read 1 to 3 bytes past the passed buffer size
items.summary: SummaryOn main, even with the guard in #9725, it's possible to have these decoders read 1 to 3 bytes past the end of the passed buffer with a suitable width/height.DetailsImagingRawDecode and the P;2L / P;4L unpackers disagree about how many bytes a line of data occupies.The raw decoder derives the line size from the bits per pixelstate->bytes = (state->xsize * state->bits + 7) / 8;and uses it both for the bounds check and to advance to the next line. For P;2L and P;4L, bits is 2 and 4 respectively.But these two rawmodes are not packed pixels but 2 or 4 bit planes, each padded to a whole number of bytes. unpackP2L computes s = (pixels + 7) / 8 and reads plane k at offset k * s, and unpackP4L does the same across four planes. Their real footprint is therefore planes * ((xsize + 7) / 8).For some widths, padding each plane separately makes this footprint larger than state->bytes. For example, at width 1, the decoder accounts for one byte, while the unpackers read two or four bytes. The decoder accepts data that is too short for the last line and on the other hand advances to subsequent lines by less than a line, so every line after the first is also read from the wrong offset.#9725's check is misshapen for this:It can reject data of the right length: 8x1 P;2L image is 2 bytes but is not accepted.It still accepts buffers shorter than the unpackers require for a given image shape.It measures the length with len(data), which is an element count rather than a byte count; e.g. memoryview(array("I", [0,0,0,0,0])) (20 bytes) is rejected while mv.tobytes() is accepted.PoC ( ghsa_p2l_p4l.py)from array import arrayfrom PIL import Image# 1 byte pastImage.frombytes("P", (1, 4), array("B", [0] * 4), "raw", "P;2L")# 3 bytes pastImage.frombytes("P", (1, 8), array("B", [0] * 8), "raw", "P;4L")is the almost-simplest reproducer.(array is needed to get ASan to reliably scream, but the overread is observable with e.g. bytes literals. Python allocates byteses with an extra trailing null byte, from an arena by default to boot, so ASan doesn't see the overread.)On my Mac, I can get ASan to scream about this withexport asan=$(clang items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
items.summary:
SummaryPIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) without sanitization, placing it at -f <infile>. A filename beginning with - is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with -dSAFER enabled).DetailsGive all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer.TypeCWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)Vulnerable Codesinfile_temp = Noneif hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):    infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validationelse:    in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()    os.close(in_fd)    infile = infile_temp    # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)# Build Ghostscript commandcommand = [    gs_binary,    "-q",    f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",    f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",    "-dBATCH",    "-dNOPAUSE",    "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection    f"-sDEVICE={device}",    f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",    "-c",    f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",    "-f",    infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for                                          # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token                                          # => argument injection (CWE-88)    "-c",    "showpage",]# ...subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns GhostscriptRoot cause.When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f  position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.AffectedPillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included).Component: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py, Ghostscript() — infile = fp.name, and the command list entry "-f", infile.Suggested fixNormalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (-/--) or as an argument-file token (@):    if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):        infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.nameos.path.abspath() guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading - or @ can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The else branch already builds a safe tempfile.mkstemp() path and needs no change.PoCdockerfile, Default run shows the argument-injection demo (poc.py); for the RCE PoC run python3 poc-rce.py.FROM ubuntu:24.04RUN apt updateRUN apt install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv ghostscript ca-certificatesRUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*RUN python3 -m venv /venv && /venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip Pillow==12.3.0ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATHWORKDIR /pocCOPY poc.py .COPY poc-rce.py .COPY arg .CMD ["python3", "poc.py"]poc.pyimport osfrom PIL import Image############################################################################################# Attacker controlled file############################################################################################EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"name = "-h"with open(name, "wb") as f:    f.write(EPS)############################################################################################print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}")im = Image.open(name)print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'")try:    im.load()except Exception as e:    print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")print("CWE-88: argument injection; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name")print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.")print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't display `help`")poc-rce.pyimport osfrom PIL import Image############################################################################################# Attacker controll

items.title: [pypdf] pypdf: Unvalidated JPEG image data loading
items.summary: ImpactAn attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to arbitrary image parsers being called. This requires loading an image which claims to use the /DCTDecode filter (JPEG data).Users which do not have the optional Pillow dependency installed in their environment are not affected.PatchesThis has been fixed in pypdf==6.21.1.WorkaroundsIf you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR #4222.Referenceshttps://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/security/advisories/GHSA-5hx5-vpf9-5wcvhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-113786https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4222https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/commit/512d8eb94eb04be1d1c90504e6da2dcef8679e07https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.21.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5hx5-vpf9-5wcv
